subject: mathematics
question_text: Show that the relation "parallel", defined on the set of all straight lines in a plane, is an equivalence relation.

mark_split.label: Show the relation is reflexive and symmetric
Show it is transitive and state the conclusion

recall_prompt: Say how you would answer this — name the three properties you check, and say what convention you use for the word parallel.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Show the relation is reflexive and symmetric
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name the convention before the reflexive check, because the reflexive check depends on it.
lines: Let L be the set of all straight lines in a plane and let R = {(l, m) : l ∈ L, m ∈ L, l ∥ m}.
Use the usual convention that a line is parallel to itself, so two lines are parallel exactly when they have the same direction.
Reflexive: l ∥ l for every line l ∈ L, so (l, l) ∈ R.
Symmetric: if l ∥ m then l and m have the same direction, so m ∥ l and (m, l) ∈ R.

recall.must_convey: That a line is taken to be parallel to itself, giving reflexivity, and that same direction works both ways, giving symmetry.
accept: a line is parallel to itself so the relation is reflexive
parallel means same direction and that works both ways so it is symmetric
if l is parallel to m then m is parallel to l
oke line daani tho ne parallel ani teesukuntam, so reflexive
state the convention first then check reflexive and symmetric

steps.why: Reflexivity holds only because of the convention that a line is parallel to itself. If parallel lines were required to be distinct, no pair (l, l) would belong to R and the relation would fail at the first property.
common_mistakes: Taking "parallel" to mean "distinct lines that never meet", which makes the relation fail to be reflexive.
Proving symmetry with one drawn example instead of for any two lines l and m.
Checking the properties on a pair of lines rather than on the whole set L.
steps.memory_tip: Parallel lines are the lines with the same direction, and "same direction" behaves in the same way as equality.

steps.label: Show it is transitive and state the conclusion
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The last line has to use the words "equivalence relation"; three checks with no conclusion is an incomplete answer.
lines: Transitive: let l ∥ m and m ∥ n, where l, m, n ∈ L.
Then l has the direction of m, and m has the direction of n.
So l and n have the same direction, that is l ∥ n and (l, n) ∈ R.

lines.text: ∴ R is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so "parallel" is an equivalence relation on L.

recall.must_convey: That l ∥ m and m ∥ n force l and n to share m's direction, so l ∥ n, and that the relation is therefore an equivalence relation.
accept: if l is parallel to m and m is parallel to n then l is parallel to n
the same direction is passed from l to m to n
all three properties hold so it is an equivalence relation
moodu properties satisfy avuthayi kabatti equivalence relation
conclude by naming it an equivalence relation

steps.why: Both l and n have the same direction as m, so they have the same direction as each other, and transitivity takes one line of work. It also needs the same convention that a line is parallel to itself: l ∥ m and m ∥ l give l ∥ l by transitivity, and the strict definition — parallel lines must be distinct — would make l ∥ l false, so transitivity would fail without the convention.
common_mistakes: Stopping after the three checks and never stating that R is an equivalence relation.
Arguing transitivity only from "the lines never meet", which does not by itself rule out l and n being the same line.
Checking only two of the three properties.
steps.memory_tip: Check reflexive, symmetric, transitive in that order every time, then write the conclusion as a full sentence.
